title: Judges 11:29–33
context: The LORD’s Spirit comes on Jephthah, and he advances against Ammon. Before battle he makes a vow: if the LORD gives him victory, whatever comes out of his house to meet him when he returns will be the LORD’s, and he will offer it up as a burnt offering. The LORD gives a great victory. Both traditions agree that the Spirit’s empowering for deliverance does not endorse the vow. They also agree that the vow was rash, made in the language of bargaining when God had not asked for it. The wording of verse 31 is debated: whether Jephthah expected an animal or a person, and whether the clause allows dedication rather than sacrifice. These questions shape how the next section is read.

verses.text: Then the LORD’s Spirit came on Jephthah, and he passed over Gilead and Manasseh, and passed over Mizpah of Gilead, and from Mizpah of Gilead he passed over to the children of Ammon.
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD’s Spirit comes on Jephthah, and he passes through Gilead and Manasseh to confront Ammon. The Spirit empowers him for deliverance.

Arminian readers note that the Spirit’s empowering does not override Jephthah’s own choices, including the vow he is about to make.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that in Judges the Spirit empowers people for specific tasks, even flawed people, without endorsing everything they do.

Both traditions agree that the Spirit’s coming does not approve the vow that follows; empowerment for service is not the same as sanction of every act.

verses.text: Jephthah vowed a vow to the LORD, and said, “If you will indeed deliver the children of Ammon into my hand,
verses.arminianNotes:
Jephthah vows to the LORD, beginning with a condition: if God will deliver Ammon into his hand. The vow is a bargain.

Arminian readers note that the vow was Jephthah’s own initiative, not something God required; he chose to bind himself.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the vow reflects a bargaining mindset that misunderstands God’s grace, which had already been given through the Spirit.

Both traditions agree that the vow was rash (compare Proverbs 20:25), and that God had not asked for it.

verses.text: then it shall be, that whatever comes out of the doors of my house to meet me when I return in peace from the children of Ammon, it shall be the LORD’s, and I will offer it up for a burnt offering.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Jephthah vows that whatever comes out of his house to meet him on his return will be the LORD’s, and he will offer it up as a burnt offering. The wording is debated.

Arminian readers note that some interpreters think Jephthah expected an animal, while others think he anticipated a person; the Hebrew can be read either way.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that a few interpreters propose reading the clause as an alternative, dedication or sacrifice, though most take it as a single promise.

Both traditions hold the meaning cautiously and agree the vow was rash.

verses.text: So Jephthah passed over to the children of Ammon to fight against them; and the LORD delivered them into his hand.
verses.arminianNotes:
Jephthah fights Ammon, and the LORD delivers them into his hand. The victory comes from God.

Arminian readers note that God gives victory through the Spirit’s empowering, not because of the vow. God’s grace is not purchased.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that God’s deliverance does not depend on Jephthah’s bargain. The LORD acts in faithfulness to his people.

Both traditions agree that the victory should not be read as God accepting or approving the vow; God delivers his people despite their failures.

verses.text: He struck them from Aroer until you come to Minnith, even twenty cities, and to Abelcheramim, with a very great slaughter. So the children of Ammon were subdued before the children of Israel.
verses.arminianNotes:
Jephthah strikes Ammon from Aroer to Minnith, twenty cities, to Abel Keramim, and Ammon is subdued. The deliverance is complete.

Arminian readers note that God’s mercy to Israel is real, even after Israel’s repeated unfaithfulness. Deliverance is a gift.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that God’s purposes for his people are fulfilled despite the moral complexity of their deliverer. His faithfulness does not depend on human perfection.

Both traditions see in Ammon’s defeat God’s answer to Israel’s cry in chapter 10, and they read the victory alongside the tragedy that follows.
